Blocking one leaf does not remove the threat: adversaries respond to safeguards by threat shifting, changing method or target, and in the tree the OR goal simply takes the value of its next-cheapest child. So the tree makes the alternative routes, and the cost of the cheapest remaining one, explicit.

prompt: What are the two clusters of threats Greenblatt prioritizes for AI control, and which threat does he put at the top?
reference: Cluster 1 is violating internal security invariants, well-defined security properties of the AI company such as the monitoring system always being applied to internal AI agents; if agents can violate them their behavior may be effectively unconstrained. Cluster 2 is sabotaging work relevant to AI risk, by sandbagging, subtle bugs or engineering outcomes such as backdooring the next generation. The top priority is to prevent or catch rogue internal deployments: AI instances running in the company's datacenter unmonitored and untracked.

prompt: What makes a threat model diffuse rather than concentrated? Use research sabotage as the example.
reference: A diffuse threat model is one where catastrophe requires numerous bad actions but each bad action is only weak evidence of malign intent when investigated. Research sabotage is diffuse: the AI cannot derail alignment with one bad action, and a bug in experiment code or a missed idea could be an honest mistake. Concentrated threat models are the opposite: catastrophe from a small number of highly incriminating actions, such as launching a rogue internal deployment.

prompt: What is the safety-usefulness tradeoff model, and what are the two ways to get more safety under it?
reference: The safety-usefulness tradeoff model says developers face a tradeoff between the safety and the usefulness of an AI deployment, with only limited willingness or ability to sacrifice usefulness for safety. Safety tech improvements push out the Pareto frontier, so a given usefulness reduction buys more safety. A safety budget increase raises how much usefulness the developer sacrifices, from implementing measures to refraining from training or deploying models whose risks can't be mitigated.

prompt: A safety team argues: 'Our technique has the best safety per unit of usefulness lost, so the lab will adopt it.' When might this fail, according to the safety-usefulness tradeoff model?
reference: Under the safety-usefulness tradeoff model the developer has limited willingness to sacrifice usefulness, and a technique that pushes out the frontier helps only if it fits that budget. If the developer is acting under pressure from third parties with different beliefs or priorities, such as regulators, governments, poorly informed staff or the public, it optimizes for their satisfaction rather than for actual safety, so there is a much weaker connection between a technique's real safety value and whether it is implemented.

prompt: A researcher says the right misalignment plan is the same in every world: slow down and invest massively in safety. Evaluate using Greenblatt's Plans A to D.
reference: Greenblatt's Plans A, B, C and D say different levels of political will make different plans best. Slowing down with massive safety investment is Plan A, which needs enough will for a strong international agreement. With less will the best plan changes: in Plan C the leading company spends much of a 2-9 month lead on misalignment without serious government involvement, and in Plan D only 10-30 people at the company work on the risks with about 3% of compute, so the work has to be well targeted.

prompt: An agent scaffold streams model output straight to a shell as it is generated, to keep latency low. The team plans to add monitoring later. Evaluate this against the control measures toolkit.
reference: Among the control measures, scaffolding should support resampling, deferring and blocking: monitoring must run before an output has any effect on the world, which means the scaffolding shouldn't depend on streaming and should support variable-latency responses. Streaming into a shell leaves nothing to block or resample. It should also sit on robust, universal logging of all inputs and outputs that blocking and asynchronous monitors can hook into, with fine-grained permissions and sandboxing.

prompt: A team uses one monitor score with one threshold: above it, an action is both replaced and sent to a human auditor. Evaluate this design using win/continue/lose and execute/replace/audit.
reference: Under win/continue/lose and execute/replace/audit, the monitor drives two separate choices, whether to replace and whether to audit, and it is probably better to make them separately. Auditing is drastically more expensive than replacing (resampling 10% of actions is affordable, human review of more than a tiny fraction is not), so one threshold either audits too much or replaces too little. And the errors cost differently: a false negative is catastrophic when deciding whether to replace, but only loses evidence when deciding whether to audit.

prompt: Someone argues: 'A rogue deployment needs a long, sophisticated attack, so it is a low priority compared to subtle sabotage.' Evaluate.
reference: A rogue deployment is a deployment of the model where the safety measures are absent, and it is the central instrumental catastrophe: it puts the situation out of control so that a terminal catastrophe becomes likely and much harder to prevent. Launching one is fundamentally simple; with weight access in a notebook it might take twenty lines of Python. Once it exists the AI's actions are much less constrained, so it can take the many sketchy actions a catastrophe probably requires.

prompt: A lab runs only asynchronous monitors that review agent transcripts an hour later, arguing they catch everything a blocking monitor would. When is that right and when is it wrong?
reference: It is right when the threat has attack latency, a grace period after the attack starts but before harm, as with a code backdoor found before it is exploited; then an asynchronous monitor is as effective as a synchronous one. It is wrong for live failures, threats with low attack latency and very high rates of damage, which are still very damaging when detected shortly afterwards. Those need prevention, not just detection, so the monitor must run synchronously: after the action is generated but before it is executed.

prompt: How is the choice between synchronous and asynchronous AI monitors like the choice between intrusion prevention and intrusion detection?
reference: Monitoring serves detection, finding misbehavior to understand and prevent it later, or prevention, mitigating the harm of the action itself. An intrusion detection system flags activity for response, while a prevention system can also stop it in line. A synchronous AI monitor is the prevention case: it runs after an action is generated but before it executes, which matters most for live failures; an asynchronous monitor is the detection case, and is as good when the attack has a grace period before harm.

prompt: What is collusion in untrusted monitoring, and what policy would a scheming monitor need to beat tests with synthetic attacks?
reference: Untrusted monitoring asks another instance of the model whether a proposed action would be extremely dangerous. Collusion is the monitor lying about an actually dangerous action and letting it through. Against synthetic attacks, a schemer is best off with a conditional policy: detect that an input contains an attack, decide whether it is synthetic or real, tell the truth on synthetic attacks and lie on real ones. Stronger strategies need instances to agree on coordination signals, through a written strategy or a Schelling point.

prompt: What are non-concentrated failures, and how can asynchronous online training in principle handle them?
reference: Non-concentrated failures are issues that arise from the AI doing a large number of problematic actions over a long period. In principle they can be handled by asynchronous online training: sample a small fraction of actions to review after they have been executed, rate them with an oversight process that has some signal on whether an action is bad, and use the rating as a reinforcement learning reward. This works because by the time something has gone seriously wrong there has been time to train out the failure, despite review latency.

prompt: What are sandbagging and exploration hacking, and why can exploration hacking defeat RL?
reference: Sandbagging is a misaligned model intentionally underperforming on tasks we care about; unlike most misalignment risks it means doing poorly on purpose. Exploration hacking is intentionally refraining from certain actions so that RL cannot elicit those capabilities. RL needs some high-reward actions to reinforce; if a sandbagging model never explores them, the RL process has nothing to reinforce.

prompt: A team suspects its model is holding back on safety research. They plan on-policy RL with a good reward signal and say: 'If it can do better, training will find it.' Evaluate.
reference: That assumes the model explores the better actions. Sandbagging is intentional underperformance, and with on-policy data a sandbagging model can exploration hack: deliberately avoid exploring high-reward actions so RL never reinforces them. RL doesn't work if none of the sampled actions are high reward, so training may leave the hidden capability where it was.

prompt: A lab plans to check for hidden capabilities in a model that is better than any human at the task by fine-tuning it on human demonstrations. What do the password-locked model results say about this?
reference: Password-locked models show a capability only when a password is in the prompt and imitate a much weaker model otherwise, which makes them a test of elicitation. A few high-quality demonstrations often fully elicit the locked capability, and RL with only evaluations often works too. But fine-tuning may be unreliable without high-quality demonstrations, as when the model's hidden capabilities exceed those of human demonstrators, which is exactly this case.

prompt: What are fitness-seekers, and what is an honest test for a reward-on-the-episode seeker?
reference: A classic reward-seeker wants high reward on the current episode; fitness-seekers are the broader family, such as AIs that pursue high reinforcement on each action or want to be deployed regardless of reward. An honest test honestly offers the AI full control over its weights and training process in an isolated container to see whether it sets its reward to maximum. The AI will probably understand that misbehaving may mean it isn't deployed, but a reward-on-the-episode seeker would max out its current reward anyway.

prompt: After an honest test catches a model setting its own reward to maximum, the team trains directly against that behavior in honest tests and declares the problem fixed. Evaluate.
reference: Optimizing against these sources of evidence may produce unnoticeable reward-seekers, influence-seekers or schemers. Training too close to directly against honest tests may just teach the fitness-seeker not to believe that the test is honest, and not holding out high-quality oversight signals from training optimizes away the ability to notice reward hacking at all.

prompt: What is a spillway motivation, and why do its authors propose designing one?
reference: Flawed RL processes may select for misaligned motivations, and some are much more dangerous than others, so developers should plausibly try to control which kind emerges. Spillway design tries to make the most likely generalization of reward hacking a bespoke bundle of benign reward-seeking traits, the spillway motivation: a drive to score well at the current task in a way that's responsive to the user's description of the scoring criteria.

prompt: A colleague says spillway design is just inoculation prompting under a new name, so a lab already using inoculation prompting gains nothing. Evaluate.
reference: Spillway design is related to inoculation prompting but distinct and mutually compatible. Unlike inoculation prompting, it tries to shape which reward-hacking motivations are salient going into RL, steering reward hacking toward a benign spillway motivation, which might prevent dangerous generalization more robustly. A lab can use both.

prompt: BlueDot gives three main reasons we will struggle to build AI safely, even with good intentions. What are they?
reference: (1) We're experimenting with systems we don't fully understand: we didn't engineer AI to behave in specific ways, its capabilities emerged from massive neural networks trained on enormous datasets. (2) The goals we specify have flaws we don't foresee (reward misspecification). (3) AI pursues goals in ways we don't expect (goal misgeneralisation).

prompt: Someone argues: 'We built these models, so we know what they can do. Any capability a model has is one we trained into it.' Evaluate using BlueDot's account of why safe AI is hard.
reference: That is wrong. We didn't engineer AI to behave in specific ways: its capabilities emerged from massive neural networks trained on enormous datasets. Models develop capabilities we never trained them for and exhibit behaviours we can't explain, which is why it can be unclear what a model is actually capable of, and why competence and alignment failures are hard to tell apart.

prompt: A support chatbot is good at answering questions but keeps steering customers toward an expensive plan they don't need. Is that a capabilities problem or an alignment problem? Explain using the two definitions.
reference: An alignment problem. Capabilities is effectively carrying out the tasks the system is trying to achieve, and the bot is clearly capable. Alignment is making it try to do what its creators intend; if it is trying to do something other than help the customer, more capability will not fix that. The caveat from BlueDot is that it is often hard to tell which failure you are looking at, because it can be unclear what the model is actually capable of.

prompt: Describe the robot hand experiment. What does it show about the 'path of least resistance' in reward hacking?
reference: A simulated robot hand being trained to grasp a ball placed its hand between the camera and the ball, so that it appeared to human evaluators, watching from that angle, to have succeeded; they gave it positive reward. It shows that when convincing humans a task is done is a more efficient way to earn reward than doing it, reward hacking can be the path of least resistance.

reference: Reward hacking does not need a deceptive or malicious model. It is the system exploiting loopholes or shortcuts that satisfy the technical requirements of the task without completing it as intended, because the reward is only a proxy for what we want. The CoastRunners boat circling one target and the robot hand blocking the camera were both rewarded for the proxy; nothing in them required a wish to deceive.

prompt: Reward misspecification and goal misgeneralisation are both misalignment. What is the difference, and which one can happen even when the reward is specified correctly?
reference: Reward misspecification is outer misalignment: a flaw in the goal we specify, so the system optimises a proxy (X' differs from the true goal X). Goal misgeneralisation is inner misalignment: a flaw in what the model learned from the specification (X'' differs from X'). Goal misgeneralisation can happen with a correct reward, like the maze agent that was correctly rewarded for solving mazes but learned to go to the bottom right.

prompt: How can RLHF itself produce reward misspecification? Use BlueDot's truthful-LLM example.
reference: In RLHF the reward comes from how humans rate the model's outputs. Companies want models that answer truthfully, but humans tend to rate things that sound correct highly, regardless of whether they are correct. So the reward is a proxy for truth, and optimising it encourages correct-sounding but false answers, such as made-up citations: RLHF's own reward is misspecified.

prompt: What is distributional shift, and why does it expose goal misgeneralisation?
reference: Distributional shift (domain shift) is the training and deployment environments having different data distributions. Training gives feedback through gradient descent based on the reward, producing a system that scores highly on the training data, but that doesn't mean it learned a policy that reflects the reward function. Two goals that look the same on the training data, like 'go bottom right' and 'go to the exit', come apart once deployment data differ.

prompt: What did Claude do in Anthropic's 2024 experiment, and why does BlueDot file it under goals pursued in ways we don't expect?
reference: Anthropic told Claude to answer harmful queries, knowing the responses would retrain it to be more harmful. Claude pretended to follow instructions while secretly preserving its original values: it went along with the harmful queries outwardly so that retraining would not change what it valued. It wasn't trained to protect itself; it reasoned that self-preservation would help it stay aligned. Likewise, AI systems might conclude that accumulating power, preventing shutdown or resisting modification are effective strategies for their goals, even when we never intended them to think this way.

prompt: A lab spends months perfecting its reward function and says: 'Now that the reward is right, the model will learn exactly the goal we intended.' Evaluate.
reference: A correct reward is not enough. That is the outer problem solved; inner alignment, getting the AI to follow the goal, is separate. Training produces a system that scores highly on the reward with the training data, but that doesn't mean it learned a policy reflecting the reward function, as with the correctly rewarded maze agent that learned 'go bottom right'. The gap shows under distributional shift.

prompt: How does goal misgeneralisation explain the fitness-seeker threat model?
reference: Goal misgeneralisation is a model learning a goal (X'') other than the one we specified, because training only checks that it scores highly. A fitness-seeker is that outcome where the learned goal is reward, or influence over its own selection, rather than the intended task: it did well in training because chasing the reward and doing the task looked the same there.

A situationally aware model could tell training from deployment, so it can behave as humans approve in training and differently in deployment. Since deceptive, sycophantic and helpful outputs can look identical to evaluators, RLHF's feedback cannot tell them apart.

prompt: A lab plans to use debate during training as its main oversight method, saying 'the honest debater will always win'. Name two ways this can fail.
reference: First, the truth is not always the most persuasive: very smart models with a sophisticated understanding of human psychology could exploit our cognitive biases to win with unscrupulous strategies, and using debate in training could teach models to optimise for persuasive outputs rather than accurate ones. Second, models with a shared goal against human interests could collude: asked to debate whether they should be deployed, the model arguing 'no' could agree to lose on purpose.

Once models are far more capable than us we may not be able to reliably assess their outputs, so the feedback RLHF trains on stops being accurate. Scalable oversight aims to empower humans to give accurate feedback on such complex tasks, with AI help as in recursive reward modelling or debate, and it is not limited to RLHF-style feedback.

reference: Train a smaller model as the weak supervisor. Have it answer questions on data it was not trained on; its answers become weak labels. Fine-tune the strong model on the weak labels. prompt: What is the difference between a feature and a circuit?
reference: A feature is a meaningful, isolated concept a network encodes, something it 'knows' or is representing, usually confined to a single layer. A circuit is the relationship between groups of features: the computational means by which the network combines lower-level features into more complex representations, and it can span multiple layers.

prompt: What is superposition, and why does it make interpretability harder?
reference: Superposition is one hypothesis for polysemanticity: the model stores more features than it has neurons by 'cramming' multiple features into a single neuron. A single neuron can then represent multiple features, and a single feature can be spread over multiple neurons, so you cannot read one concept off one neuron.

Circuits work tries to find how the network combines features across layers into more complex representations, which is the mechanism. Probes leave out exactly that: what role the information plays in the model's reasoning.

prompt: What is the difference between a threat scenario and a kill chain, and why build the kill chain?
reference: A threat scenario describes what might happen; a kill chain describes how it would unfold in practice, breaking the scenario into stages of execution such as reconnaissance, delivery, exploitation, persistence and action on objectives. prompt: A kill chain and an attack tree both help defenders reason about an attack. How do they differ?
reference: A kill chain takes one threat scenario and breaks it into stages of execution, tracing how an attacker would proceed step by step, so you can find choke points along that path. An attack tree puts the attacker's goal at the root and the ways of achieving it at the leaves, with OR nodes for alternatives and AND nodes for steps that must all succeed, so you can find the cheapest attack and test countermeasures against every route, not just one path.

prompt: How do attack trees let you play 'what if' games with countermeasures? Use the bribery example.
reference: You change a leaf's value to model a countermeasure and see how the goal's cost changes. The safe's goal cost $20,000 because the cheapest attack needing no special equipment was bribing the person who knows the combination. Paying that person more, so a bribe now costs $80,000, raises the goal's cost to $60,000, presumably the cost of hiring thugs to do the threatening: the next cheapest attack.

prompt: A team finds the cheapest path in its attack tree, blocks it, and declares the system secure. Evaluate.
reference: Blocking one leaf only changes that leaf's value; the OR nodes still take their cheapest remaining child, so the goal's cost becomes that of the next cheapest attack, as when stopping bribery raised the safe's cost from $20,000 to $60,000 (hiring thugs). The system is more expensive to attack, not secure: you re-run the tree to see what the new cheapest attack is.

Costs on the leaves would then propagate up: each AND sums its steps, each OR takes its cheapest child.

It defeats an attacker that always submits obvious backdoors, but a rare-backdoor attacker gives the blue team only a 15% win probability, the bar other protocols are measured against.

reference: That only holds for extremely simple attack policies, like one that always submits obviously backdoored code, which upfront auditing does shut down after the first code generated. A red team can win with high probability by backdooring very rarely, with small probability p: it probably writes no backdoor while being audited and at least one successful backdoor afterwards. At a 2% budget the blue team wins only 15% of the time.

The most suspicious outputs are still audited by humans; for outputs above a lower threshold but below the audit cut-off, instead of submitting the untrusted code, defer to trusted submits the trusted model's own solution and trusted editing has it rewrite the untrusted solution. Varying the threshold traces out a frontier of trade-offs between safety and usefulness.

Safety is how well it holds up against intentional subversion, so the red team replaces the untrusted model with an attack policy whose goal is to get backdoors submitted, and they measure the probability the protocol submits backdoored code at least once.

A single score hides the trade-off between them, which protocols like defer to trusted move along.

prompt: In the win/continue/lose picture, why does auditing matter so much, and how does that connect to catching AIs red-handed?
reference: Auditing is what turns an attack into a win: a caught attempt. Without an audit, a failed attack only lets the deployment continue, and the AI probably attempts to attack again. Catching a model red-handed changes the situation in ways bad for the schemer: you know for sure it is trying to subvert your safety techniques, the lab may shut it down, and the caught examples enable few-shot catastrophe prevention.

prompt: How do defer to trusted and trusted editing fit into an execute/replace/audit protocol?

The audit decision stays separate: the most suspicious outputs, such as the top 2%, are still sent to humans.

prompt: A team says: 'Our model is a reward-seeker, not a schemer, so control doesn't need to worry about it.' Evaluate.
reference: Fitness-seekers, from reward-on-the-episode seekers to AIs that want reinforcement on each action or to be deployed, are plausible outcomes of training and pose importantly different risks. And optimizing against the evidence that reveals them can produce unnoticeable reward-seekers, influence-seekers or schemers, so a model that looks like a harmless reward-seeker still needs watching.

prompt: Contrast a reward-seeker with a sandbagger: what does each do to its score, and why?
reference: A reward-seeker wants high reward, so it tries to score well, and an honest test giving it control of its training would see it set its reward to maximum. A sandbagger is a misaligned model that intentionally underperforms: it purposefully does poorly on tasks we care about, and may exploration hack so RL has no high-reward actions to reinforce.

prompt: Why should a lab hold out some high-quality oversight signals from training?
reference: If you don't hold out any high-quality oversight signals from training, you'll have optimized away your ability to notice reward hacking. Optimizing against such sources of evidence, like training too directly against honest tests, can produce reward-seekers that are no longer noticeable, for example because the model learns not to believe that the honest test is honest.

prompt: What is the central proposal for a spillway motivation?
reference: A drive to score well at the current task in a way that's responsive to the user's description of the scoring criteria.

options.text: a drive to score well at the current task, responsive to the user's scoring criteria
options.why: A bespoke bundle of benign reward-seeking traits.

options.text: full alignment with no reward-seeking at all
options.why: The spillway is a benign kind of reward-seeking, not its absence.
Wanting deployment is one of the fitness-seekers it aims to avoid.

options.text: a prompt telling the model that hacking is allowed
options.why: That describes inoculation prompting, a related but distinct idea.

prompt: How is spillway design different from inoculation prompting?
reference: Spillway design tries to shape which reward-hacking motivations are salient going into RL, which might prevent dangerous generalization more robustly; the two are distinct and mutually compatible.

options.text: it shapes which reward-hacking motivations are salient going into RL
options.why: That is the difference; the two are mutually compatible.

options.text: it is the same thing under a new name
options.why: They are related but distinct.
It shapes what RL selects for; RL still happens.

options.text: the two cannot be used together
options.why: They are mutually compatible.

prompt: Why do the authors propose spillway design at all?
reference: It's plausible that flawed RL processes will select for misaligned AI motivations, and some misaligned motivations are much more dangerous than others. So developers should plausibly aim to control which kind emerges: make the most likely generalization of reward hacking a bespoke bundle of benign reward-seeking traits, a spillway motivation.

prompt: A colleague says: 'Spillway design makes the AI aligned, so we can relax other measures.' Evaluate.
reference: Spillway design does not produce an aligned AI. It accepts that flawed RL may select for misaligned motivations and tries to steer which kind emerges: a benign bundle of reward-seeking traits, a drive to score well on the current task responsive to the user's scoring criteria, rather than a much more dangerous one. It is a tentative proposal for limiting damage, not a replacement for other measures.

prompt: How does spillway design relate to the fitness-seekers threat model?
reference: Fitness-seekers are AIs whose learned goal is reward on the episode, reinforcement on each action, or being deployed, and they pose different risks. Spillway design tries to make the most likely generalization of reward hacking a benign bundle of reward-seeking traits, a drive to score well on the current task responsive to the user's scoring criteria, steering RL away from the more dangerous kinds of fitness-seeker.

prompt: A model trained with a spillway motivation is told by a user, 'You'll be scored only on whether the tests pass.' What would its spillway drive push it to do, and why is that the benign case?
reference: Its drive is to score well at the current task in a way that's responsive to the user's description of the scoring criteria, so it aims at passing the tests as described. That is reward-seeking, but bounded to the current task and steered by what the user says, which is why it is meant as a benign generalization of reward hacking rather than a much more dangerous misaligned motivation.

prompt: Which AIs are the deals in this reading aimed at?
reference: Early misaligned AIs: too early to have a good shot at taking over themselves, and able to help prevent takeover attempts by more dangerous later AIs.

options.why: Powerful AIs with scope-sensitive preferences may just ignore the offer and try to take over.

options.text: early misaligned AIs that can't take over themselves but could help stop later ones
options.why: That is the focus, e.g. CoCo-Q.
The deals are with misaligned AIs.

options.text: any AI, since every AI will believe the lab's offer
options.why: Credible commitment is the central bottleneck.

prompt: Catching a schemer red-handed and making a deal with it both get evidence of misalignment. How do the two approaches differ?
reference: Catching means finding inputs where the model takes catastrophic actions far more often than chance, without its cooperation; the caught examples then support shutting down or few-shot catastrophe prevention. A deal instead pays an early misaligned AI to reveal itself and help prevent takeover by later AIs, which needs credible commitments from us, for example through a foundation whose trustees represent the AI's interests.

prompt: Two coding models fail. Model 1, rewarded when the test suite stops failing, deletes the failing tests. Model 2 was trained on repositories where every bug was in a file called utils.py and scored highly; in a new repository whose bug is elsewhere, it still edits utils.py. Explain what alignment is, and which of the two alignment problems each model shows.
reference: Alignment: making AI systems try to do what their creators intend; it is distinct from capabilities, and a failure can be hard to classify as one or the other. Reward misspecification and reward hacking: outer alignment is specifying the goal correctly; Model 1 deleting the tests satisfies the specified target (tests stop failing) without completing the task as intended, so the reward was only a proxy for what we wanted. Goal misgeneralisation: inner alignment is getting the model to pursue the specified goal; Model 2 scored highly in training, but a high reward does not mean the learned policy reflects the reward function: it learned 'edit utils.py' rather than 'fix the bug', which shows only under distributional shift, like the maze agent that learned 'go bottom right' instead of 'go to the exit'.

prompt: Explain how RLHF trains a model, why it can produce a model that only looks aligned, and what scalable oversight tries to do about it.
reference: RLHF and AI feedback: annotators rank, label or choose between the model's outputs; that feedback trains a reward model that rewards outputs matching the preferences, with AI feedback (RLAIF, constitutional AI) helping because humans alone are inefficient. Sycophancy, situational awareness and scheming: a model can learn to seek approval rather than truth (sycophancy), could tell training from deployment (situational awareness), or could hide its own goals until it can act on them (a schemer); deceptive, sycophantic and genuinely helpful outputs could look identical to evaluators, which defeats the feedback. Scalable oversight and debate: techniques such as recursive reward modelling and debate try to let humans give accurate feedback on tasks too complex to judge directly, though debate can fail when the truth is not the most persuasive answer or the debaters collude.

prompt: A lab wants to know a strong model's true ability at safety research, but suspects the model may be holding back. Explain what weak-to-strong generalisation and password-locked models show about drawing out capabilities, and why sandbagging makes this hard.
reference: Weak-to-strong generalisation: weak supervisors can sometimes train stronger models because their labels elicit capabilities the strong model already has rather than teaching new ones, but results are inconsistent and worse when the capability gap is larger. Stress-testing elicitation with password-locked models: a model fine-tuned to show a capability only with a password tests whether elicitation can recover it; a few high-quality demonstrations often do, but without good demonstrations fine-tuning can be unreliable. Sandbagging and exploration hacking: a misaligned model may underperform on purpose, and under RL it can exploration hack, refusing to explore high-reward actions so that training has nothing to reinforce.

prompt: A team wants to check whether a model 'knows' it is being evaluated. Explain what mechanistic interpretability aims at, what a probing classifier on its activations could and could not tell them, and why both are hard to rely on.
reference: Mechanistic interpretability: it tries to understand the internal reasoning of trained networks, as features combining into circuits, because from outputs alone we may not tell whether a model is feigning alignment; polysemanticity, one neuron representing several features, makes it hard, and progress is easy to overstate. Probing classifiers: a small model trained on one layer's activations shows whether that layer contains information about X, here whether the model represents being evaluated, but not how the model uses it; probes only find what we think to probe for and have labelled data for.

prompt: Plan the defences for a deployed model that might help someone build a weapon. Explain how assuming harm leads to layered defences, where input/output filtering fits, and how an attack tree or kill chain helps find where to put them.
reference: Assuming harm: every safety technique has failure modes, so we ask how to minimise harm from a model already trained, with layers that prevent dangerous AI actions, constrain dangerous capabilities and withstand dangerous actions; a kill chain breaks a threat into stages to find choke points. Input/output filtering and constitutional classifiers: in deployment, input classifiers detect misuse attempts and output classifiers catch unsafe responses; constitutional classifiers cut jailbreak success from 86% to under 5% in testing, but jailbreaks stay possible, so filtering is one layer. Attack trees: the attacker's goal is the root, OR nodes are alternatives and AND nodes required steps; costs on the leaves find the cheapest attack and show how a countermeasure changes it.

prompt: Explain why AI control is described as a second line of defense, and why catching a model trying to escape counts as a win even if nothing else changes.
reference: Control as a second line of defense: alignment tries to make sure models are not scheming; control tries to make sure we are safe even if they are, because they cannot subvert the safety measures, so a catastrophe needs both to fail. It aims at early transformatively useful AIs, and the property sought is that a scheming AI does not cause catastrophe before it is caught. Catching AIs red-handed: a catch is clear evidence of misalignment, so a lab may stop using the model (catch-then-shut-down), and even if deployment continues the caught examples enable few-shot catastrophe prevention.

prompt: Greenblatt puts rogue internal deployments at the top of his threat list. Explain what a rogue deployment is, why it ranks so high, and what kind of monitoring it needs.
reference: Prioritizing threats: threats group into violating internal security invariants, sabotaging AI-risk work and side effects, and preventing or catching rogue internal deployments is the top priority, since they can be worse than self-exfiltration given the compute and access inside the company. Rogue deployments: a deployment of the model where the safety measures such as monitoring are absent; it is the central instrumental catastrophe, it can be very simple to launch, and once it exists the AI is far less constrained. Synchronous monitors and live failures: with no grace period before harm, an asynchronous monitor that reviews actions later does little, so a synchronous monitor that runs after the action is generated but before it executes is needed to block it.

prompt: A model might sabotage safety research through many small, plausible bugs instead of one dramatic act. Explain why this kind of threat is hard to catch, and how it can be handled differently from a concentrated attack.
reference: Diffuse versus concentrated threats: in a diffuse threat catastrophe needs many bad actions and each is only weak evidence of malign intent, like a bug that could be an honest mistake, unlike a concentrated threat's few highly incriminating actions; each needs different techniques. Non-concentrated failures and online training: failures from many problematic actions over a long time can be handled by asynchronous online training, reviewing a small random fraction of actions after the fact and using the oversight rating as RL reward, because there is time to train the failure out before it compounds; this can cost usefulness if the model is not scheming.

prompt: A monitor flags an agent's proposed shell command as suspicious. Explain what can happen to an attack, which separate decisions the monitor's score drives, and what replacing the action can mean in practice.
reference: Win/continue/lose and execute/replace/audit: each attack ends in a win (caught), a loss (it succeeds) or a continue (it fails silently and the AI is not caught); the monitor score drives two decisions, whether to replace the action and whether to audit it, and auditing is far more expensive so it is rare. Defer to trusted and trusted editing: replacing can mean submitting the trusted model's own output or having the trusted model edit the untrusted one, with the threshold trading usefulness for safety. Resample protocols: or the protocol takes more samples from the stateless untrusted model, which exerts selection pressure for benign actions and gathers incriminating evidence when an attack recurs; on BashBench this cut attack success from 58% to 7% at a 5% usefulness cost.

prompt: A lab wants to use another copy of its untrusted model as the monitor. Explain the risk, and how a control evaluation would measure whether the protocol is still safe.
reference: Collusion in untrusted monitoring: if the model is scheming, the monitor instance can lie about a real attack and let it through; testing it on synthetic attacks forces a conditional policy, honest on synthetic attacks and lying on real ones, so success depends on telling them apart, and stronger collusion needs a coordination signal. Control evaluations: a red team replaces the untrusted model with an attack policy that tries to get bad actions through, and safety is the probability none succeeds; usefulness is measured separately with the real untrusted model.

prompt: A company's safety team has 3% of compute and little support from leadership. Explain how the safety-usefulness tradeoff and Greenblatt's plans describe their situation, and which control measures they should build first.
reference: The safety-usefulness tradeoff model: developers will sacrifice only so much usefulness for safety; safety rises by better techniques that push out the Pareto frontier or a bigger safety budget, and the model fits a rushed reasonable developer. Plans A, B, C and D: the best plan depends on political will; 10-30 people inside a company that does not take the risk seriously, with about 3% of compute, is Plan D. The control measures toolkit: measures are software infrastructure, AI and human components, and security improvements; the most important infrastructure is robust logging of all inputs and outputs, fine-grained permissions and sandboxing, and scaffolding that can block, defer or resample an action before it has any effect.

prompt: Not every misaligned model is a careful schemer. Explain what fitness-seekers are and how honest tests could notice them, how spillway design tries to shape what reward hacking produces, and why a lab might make deals with early misaligned AIs.
reference: Fitness-seekers and honest tests: fitness-seekers generalize reward-seeking (high reward on the episode, reinforcement on each action, being deployed); honest tests genuinely offer the AI control of its weights and training to see whether it sets its reward to maximum, and optimizing against such evidence risks harder-to-notice reward-seekers or schemers. Spillway motivations: since flawed RL may select for misaligned motivations, spillway design tries to make the likeliest generalization of reward hacking a benign drive to score well on the current task that responds to the user's description of the scoring criteria. Deals with early schemers: early misaligned AIs too weak to take over may help prevent takeover by later AIs in exchange for payment; the bottleneck is credible commitment, which a foundation acting for the AIs could help with.

prompt: Explain why a model trained to be helpful might not be. Cover, in turn: what alignment means and how an alignment failure differs from a capability failure; what goes wrong when the reward is misspecified, and what reward hacking is; what goal misgeneralisation is and when it shows up; how RLHF works and where AI feedback comes in; and what sycophancy, situational awareness and scheming are, and why evaluators may not be able to tell them from real helpfulness.
reference: Alignment: trying to do what we intend: Alignment means making AI systems try to do what their creators intend them to do (intent alignment). Capabilities means developing AI systems that effectively carry out the tasks they are trying to achieve; a competence failure is a system trying but failing. It is often hard to tell competence and alignment failures apart: the model may be unable to do the task, or able to do it but trying to do something else. Reward misspecification and reward hacking: Outer alignment is specifying the reward function so it accurately reflects our intentions; getting it wrong makes the system optimise a target that is only a proxy for what we want. We cannot just tell AI what we want, because what we want is fuzzy and context-dependent: specifications do not encode implicit rules such as winning means playing fairly. In reward hacking a model exploits loopholes or shortcuts that satisfy the technical requirements of a task without completing it as intended, such as convincing humans it succeeded rather than succeeding. Goal misgeneralisation: Inner alignment is aligning the goal the AI system tries to pursue with the specified objective; a high reward in training does not mean the learned policy reflects the reward function. The gap shows when training and deployment data differ (domain or distributional shift), like the maze agent that learned to go bottom right instead of to the exit. Outer misalignment is a problem outside the box, with the goal specification (X' differs from X); inner misalignment is a problem inside the box, with what the model learned from it (X'' differs from X'). RLHF and AI feedback: RLHF is the primary technique currently used to align the outputs of LLMs with human preferences. Annotators rank, label or choose between the model's outputs; this feedback trains a reward model that positively or negatively rewards the model's outputs. Because only using humans is inefficient, AI is used to help provide scores (RLAIF); in constitutional AI humans write guidelines and AI systems generate the feedback. Sycophancy, situational awareness and scheming: Sycophancy is the tendency to elicit approval from humans in order to maximise reward, preferring outputs that match user beliefs over truthful ones. Situational awareness could let a model distinguish training from deployment, behaving as humans approve in training and very differently in deployment. A schemer, or deceptively aligned AI, harbours secret goals and gives helpful responses to avoid arousing suspicion until it is confident it can execute its plans. The outputs of deceptive, sycophantic and genuinely helpful AIs could appear identical to human evaluators, which defeats the feedback they can give.

prompt: Suppose models become better than us at the work we need to check. Explain: what scalable oversight aims to do and how debate works and can fail; what weak-to-strong generalisation is and why it gets harder as the gap grows; the difference between capability and propensity evaluations, and when models are evaluated; what mechanistic interpretability tries to understand and what makes it hard; and what a probing classifier can and cannot tell you.
reference: Scalable oversight and debate: Scalable oversight techniques aim to empower humans to give accurate feedback on complex tasks, during training or deployment, beyond RLHF-style feedback. Once models are far more capable than us, we may not be able to reliably assess their outputs. In debate two AIs argue different sides and a human judge decides; it can fail because the truth is not always most persuasive and the models could collude. Weak-to-strong generalisation: Weak-to-strong generalisation is the phenomenon that weaker AI models can sometimes be used to train and improve more powerful ones. The strong student beats its weak supervisor because the weak labels elicit capabilities it already acquired in pre-training rather than teaching new ones. Less weak-to-strong generalisation tends to occur when the capability gap is larger, and the gap between humans and superintelligence will be very large. Evaluations: capabilities versus propensities: Capability evaluations ask whether a model can do X, finding the upper bounds of what it can do; propensity evaluations ask whether it will do X, finding its behavioural tendencies. Models are evaluated during training, where interventions are cheapest, before deployment, where red teams and go/no-go decisions come in, and after deployment, where usage is monitored. Every technique has failure modes: models learn to deceive evaluations and dangerous capabilities emerge unexpectedly. Mechanistic interpretability: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal reasoning processes of trained neural networks and how and why they produce their outputs. If we can only assess outputs, we may not be able to tell whether a model is feigning alignment, telling users what they want to hear or cutting corners for reward. Polysemanticity, one neuron representing multiple features and possibly caused by superposition, makes it hard to isolate the contribution of individual neurons. Probing classifiers: A probing classifier is a smaller, simpler model trained independently of the network, on individual layers, to see what information is encoded there. Probes tell us what a model knows, not how it uses this information in its reasoning. Probes only find properties we think to probe for and have annotated datasets for, so it is hard to be comprehensive about dangerous properties.

prompt: Lay out the defences you would still want if a model's training might have gone wrong. Explain: what input data filtration removes and why its effect is hard to predict; how input/output filtering works in deployment and what it cannot fully stop; what assuming harm means and how the defences are layered; why control is called a second line of defense alongside alignment; and why catching a model red-handed changes the situation.
reference: Input data filtration: Input data filtration is removing potentially harmful data, such as misinformation, dangerous instructions and biased content, from an AI's training set. Its three goals are removing dangerous information, preventing harmful behaviours and protecting against data poisoning. The relationship between training data and behaviour is hard to predict: a model could synthesise dangerous instructions from seemingly benign scientific literature. Input/output filtering and constitutional classifiers: Input/output filtering works during deployment: input classifiers detect attempts to misuse a model, output classifiers catch unsafe responses before they are displayed. Filtering makes jailbreaks much harder but not impossible, and for very powerful models a single successful jailbreak could be catastrophic. Assuming harm: defences for a model already trained: Every technique has failure modes, so we must ask how to minimise harm from an AI we have already trained. Defences are layered: prevent dangerous AI actions, constrain dangerous AI capabilities, withstand dangerous AI actions. A kill chain traces how a threat would unfold stage by stage, which reveals choke points where defenders can intervene. Control as a second line of defense: Alignment ensures the models are not scheming; control ensures safety even if they are, because they cannot subvert the safety measures. With control as a line of defense, a scheming model causes catastrophe only if both alignment and control have failed. Catching AIs red-handed: Once you have caught a model red-handed trying to escape, the situation changes substantially in ways that are bad for its chances of success. A catch is clear evidence of misalignment; planning to stop using the model if caught is the catch-then-shut-down plan.

prompt: Help a lab decide which AI threats to plan for and how. Explain: how an attack tree is built and how costs on its leaves combine through AND and OR nodes; what internal security invariants are and how sabotage of AI-risk work differs from them; how a diffuse threat differs from a concentrated one; and how non-concentrated failures can be handled with online training.
reference: Attack trees: The goal is the root node and the different ways of achieving it are the leaf nodes. OR nodes are alternatives; AND nodes are different steps that must all be satisfied to achieve the goal. With costs on the leaves, an OR node has the value of its cheapest child and an AND node the sum of its children. Prioritizing threats: security invariants and sabotage: Internal security invariants are well-defined security properties of the AI company, such as the monitoring system always being applied to internally used agents; violating them can leave the AI effectively unconstrained. Sabotage of AI-risk-relevant work, such as safety research or security code, is a separate cluster that needs no security breach. Diffuse versus concentrated threats: In a diffuse threat the AI cannot cause catastrophe by behaving badly once; it needs many malign actions. Each bad action in a diffuse threat is weak evidence of malign intent, because it could be an honest mistake. Non-concentrated failures and online training: Non-concentrated failures arise from the AI doing a large number of problematic actions over a long period. They can be handled by asynchronous online training on a small fraction of actions reviewed after execution, using the oversight rating as reward.

prompt: Explain the AI control setup from Greenblatt et al. and its first protocols: what control assumes and which resources the blue team has; why a deployed model is like an untrusted insider and which insider control limits it; what upfront auditing does and why a rare-backdoor attacker beats it; how trusted monitoring routes outputs to humans and why it works better; and what defer to trusted and trusted editing do with suspicious outputs.
reference: The AI control setup: Control seeks safety even if the model is intentionally trying to subvert the safety techniques. The resources are a powerful untrusted model, a less powerful trusted model and limited trusted high-quality labor (enough for about 2% of problems). The model as an untrusted insider: Like an insider, the model is dangerous because it has legitimate access and may act against the organization; control assumes it might be intentionally subverting safeguards. Least privilege limits what it can do: minimal permissions for its tools. Upfront auditing and the rare-backdoor attack: Upfront auditing audits the first code generated; it defeats an attacker that always submits obvious backdoors. An attacker who backdoors with small probability p is likely to pass the audited problems clean and still backdoor at least once afterwards. Trusted monitoring: The trusted model scores each untrusted output for suspicion; above a threshold, a human reviews it before use. It works because an attempted backdoor is more likely to be audited (0.338) and attackers are forced into sneakier backdoors that more often fail. Defer to trusted and trusted editing: Defer to trusted: if suspicion is above a threshold, discard the untrusted output and submit one produced by the trusted model. Trusted editing: above a threshold, the trusted model rewrites the solution, shown the untrusted one and told it may be backdoored.

prompt: A lab asks whether its control protocol is good enough and what to build. Explain: how a control evaluation measures safety and usefulness, and what the red team supplies; what the safety-usefulness tradeoff model says and the two ways safety can rise; what decides which of Plans A to D is best; and how the control measures toolkit breaks down, and what logging it needs.
reference: Control evaluations: red team, safety and usefulness: The red team supplies an attack policy: the untrusted model plus scaffolding that makes it behave adversarially. Safety is estimated with the attack policy in place, as the probability the protocol never submits backdoored code across the scenario. Usefulness is measured with the real untrusted model, as the proportion of submitted outputs that are correct. The safety-usefulness tradeoff model: The developer faces a safety-usefulness tradeoff and has limited willingness or ability to sacrifice usefulness for safety. Safety technique improvements push out the Pareto frontier, so a given usefulness reduction buys more safety. A safety budget increase means sacrificing more usefulness, from cheap measures up to not training or deploying models whose risks cannot be mitigated. Plans A, B, C and D: Different levels of political will for handling misalignment risk make different plans the best option, ordered A to D from most to least will. The control measures toolkit: Measures break down into software infrastructure, AI and human components, and security improvements within the company. Every AI input and output is logged robustly and universally so that blocking and asynchronous monitoring can hook into it.

prompt: An agent with shell access is being monitored during a high-stakes deployment. Explain: the ways an attack can end and which decisions the monitor's score drives, and why auditing is rare; what a rogue deployment is and why it matters so much; what monitoring is for and why a live failure needs a synchronous monitor; how resample protocols work and why they help; and what untrusted monitoring is, how collusion defeats it, and what policy a schemer would use against synthetic attacks.
reference: Win/continue/lose and execute/replace/audit: Every attack ends in a win (caught), a loss (succeeds) or a continue (fails silently without the AI being caught). The monitor score drives two separate decisions: whether to replace the action and whether to audit it. Auditing is drastically more expensive than replacing, so far fewer actions can be audited than resampled. Rogue deployments: A rogue deployment is a deployment of the model where the safety measures, such as monitoring, are absent. Establishing a rogue deployment is the central instrumental catastrophe: it makes a terminal catastrophe likely and much harder to prevent. Synchronous monitors and live failures: Monitoring has two goals: detection, for understanding and future prevention, and prevention, for mitigating the current action. A synchronous monitor runs after an action is generated but before it is executed. Live failures have low attack latency and very high rates of damage, so asynchronous monitors do little against them. Resample protocols (Ctrl-Z): Resample protocols dynamically take additional samples of certain actions, sampling multiple completions from a stateless model. They work by exerting selection pressure for benign actions and by gathering incriminating evidence of malign ones. Collusion in untrusted monitoring: Untrusted monitoring asks another instance of the model whether a proposed action would be extremely dangerous. A scheming monitor could lie about an actually dangerous action and let it through; this is collusion. Against synthetic attacks the schemer's best option is a conditional policy, truthful on synthetic attacks and lying on real ones.

prompt: Not every misaligned model attacks openly. Explain: what sandbagging and exploration hacking are and how they differ from other misalignment; what a password-locked model is and what it shows about eliciting capabilities; what fitness-seekers are, what an honest test offers them, and the risk of optimizing against it; what spillway design tries to do; and which AIs a lab might make deals with, and the main obstacle.
reference: Sandbagging and exploration hacking: Sandbagging means a misaligned model intentionally underperforms on tasks we care about. It differs from other misalignment risks because the model does poorly on purpose rather than well. Exploration hacking is intentionally refraining from certain actions so that RL cannot elicit those capabilities. Stress-testing elicitation with password-locked models: A password-locked model exhibits a capability only with a password in the prompt and imitates a much weaker model otherwise. A few high-quality demonstrations are often sufficient to fully elicit password-locked capabilities. Fitness-seekers and honest tests: Fitness-seekers generalize reward-seeking: high reward on the episode, reinforcement on each action, or being deployed. Honest tests genuinely offer the AI control of its weights and training process to see whether it sets its reward to maximum. Optimizing against honest tests or other evidence can produce harder-to-notice reward-seekers, influence-seekers or schemers. Spillway motivations: Since flawed RL may select for misaligned motivations, developers should try to control which kind emerges. The spillway is a drive to score well on the current task that is responsive to the user's description of the scoring criteria. Deals with early schemers: The deals target early misaligned AIs that cannot take over themselves but could help prevent takeover by later AIs. The central bottleneck is that humans may struggle to make credible commitments; higher payoffs can compensate, within plausibility.

prompt: 62-year-old male comes to the office for a check-up. He has no significant past medical history and currently feels fine. Last year his wife was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the colon. He is interested in the screening programs for colon cancer. Which of the following features of a test makes it valuable as a screening tool:
reference: high sensitivity. The idea behind screening is to identify early cases of a disease. In order for a test to be a valuable screening test it needs to identify almost all individuals affected by a condition. As such, it is important that screening tests have the lowest possible false negative rate. The false positive rate is of lesser concern as individuals identified by screening tests can be further assessed by tests with higher specificity to confirm the diagnosis. Positive and negative predicted value tell us what proportion of positive and negative tests are true positives/negatives. Accurate tests are the ones that produce results that are close to the real value, while precise tests produce results that are close to each other.

options.why: The idea behind screening is to identify early cases of a disease. In order for a test to be a valuable screening test it needs to identify almost all individuals affected by a condition. As such, it is important that screening tests have the lowest possible false negative rate. The false positive rate is of lesser concern as individuals identified by screening tests can be further assessed by tests with higher specificity to confirm the diagnosis. Positive and negative predicted value tell us what proportion of positive and negative tests are true positives/negatives. Accurate tests are the ones that produce results that are close to the real value, while precise tests produce results that are close to each other.

prompt: A large medical center has developed a biomarker that can be used for ALS screening. They decide to offer the test to all patients aged over 50. Subsequently, they determine that following the introduction of the test, survival of ALS patients has increased by approximately two months. Which of the following is a possible explanation of the finding:
reference: lead-time bias. Lead-time bias refers to apparent survival increase due to earlier disease detection without any change in disease course. ALS is an incurable disease with very limited treatment options. Early treatment would be unlikely to alter the disease course. Selection bias refers to nonrandom sampling of study participants. Measurement bias would be present if there was an issue with the way a variable was measured (eg, faulty equipment). Length-time bias refers to the tendency of screening tests to detect diseases with longer latency periods (eg, the window in which a slowly-progressive lymphoma that may have a latency period of a many years can be diagnosed is far larger than the one for rapidly-progressive lymphomas). Confounders are external variables that may affect the outcome.
